what_its_for: Acetazolamide is used to treat several conditions. It helps reduce fluid pressure in your eyes (glaucoma), prevents and treats altitude sickness (when climbing to high elevations), controls certain types of seizures (epilepsy), and reduces fluid buildup in the brain or body (edema). Your doctor may also use it for other conditions not listed here.
how_to_take: Take acetazolamide by mouth exactly as your doctor prescribed. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help if it upsets your stomach. Swallow the extended-release capsules (Diamox Sequels) whole — do not crush, chew, or break them open. If you have trouble swallowing regular tablets, you may crush them and mix with a small amount of sweet liquid like honey or maple syrup. Drink plenty of water throughout the day while taking this medicine. Try to take it at the same time(s) each day to keep a steady level in your body.
dosing: Doses vary widely depending on what condition is being treated. Common adult doses range from 125 mg to 1,000 mg per day, split into 1 to 4 doses depending on your condition. For altitude sickness prevention, it is often taken 1 to 2 days before going to high altitude and continued for 2 days after arriving. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose on your own. Your doctor will find the right dose for you based on your condition and how well your kidneys are working.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store acetazolamide tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the label. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medication.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking acetazolamide, as it can increase dizziness and other side effects. Be careful driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, since it can cause drowsiness or dizziness. Avoid prolonged time in the sun or heat, as acetazolamide can make you more sensitive to sunlight and may affect your body's ability to handle high temperatures. Avoid high-sodium foods or salt substitutes unless your doctor approves them. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, including vitamins and supplements, because many drugs can interact with acetazolamide.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: a severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling skin; difficulty breathing or swallowing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; unusual bleeding or bruising; severe muscle pain or weakness; dark urine or yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems); signs of low potassium such as muscle cramps, irregular heartbeat, or extreme weakness; confusion or unusual mood changes; painful or difficult urination or blood in your urine; or signs of a serious blood disorder such as fever, chills, or sore throat that won't go away. Also call your doctor if you develop tingling or numbness in your hands and feet that bothers you, or if your condition does not improve.
when_it_works: How quickly acetazolamide works depends on what it is being used for. For glaucoma, you may notice effects within 1 to 2 hours. For altitude sickness prevention, it works best when started 1 to 2 days before going to high altitude. For seizures or fluid buildup (edema), it may take several days to see the full benefit. Keep taking it as prescribed even if you feel fine, and talk to your doctor before stopping.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): You may be more sensitive to the side effects of acetazolamide, especially dizziness, confusion, and kidney effects. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Pregnancy: Acetazolamide may harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of this medicine can pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while taking this medicine. Children: Dosing in children is based on body weight. Follow your doctor's instructions carefully. Kidney or liver problems: This medicine should be used with great caution or avoided if you have kidney or liver disease. Your doctor will check your kidney function before and during treatment.
